title: TSU female dorm sparks questions over real construction progress; OFDM admits, clarifies delays
author: Andrei P. Opeña
excerpt: Concerns have been raised over the real construction progress of the Tarlac State University (TSU) Female Dormitory currently being built at the Lucinda Campus to provide female students and employees with a secure, accessible, and…
body:
Concerns have been raised over the real construction progress of the Tarlac State University (TSU) Female Dormitory currently being built at the Lucinda Campus to provide female students and employees with a secure, accessible, and conducive on-campus living environment pursuant to Republic Act No. 11396 or the Land Use Development and Infrastructure Plan (LUDIP) Law.

The concerns stemmed from the budget allocation of TSU under the General Appropriations Act (GAA) for the 2026 fiscal year, which allotted a 50-million-peso budget for the construction of the project’s Phase III despite its actual physical framework “looking as if it were still in its initial phase of construction.” 

To be built on the 2,592-square-meter lot donated by the Serafin and Lucinda David Family to TSU intended for the construction of male and female dormitories, the design phase of the project was 100% accomplished by 2023 with an approved budget for the first phase amounting to 40 million pesos per the university’s annual financial report of that year.

In TSU’s 2024 annual report, however, the project remained under the design phase but its approved contract budget for its Phase I was indicated to have amounted to only 30 million pesos, 10 million lower than what was specified in the 2023 financial report. 

Meanwhile, in the first quarter of 2025, Phase II of the project was allocated a 40-million-peso budget despite the fact that plans for Phase I were only executed on January 13, 2025, as the contractor officially mobilized to the project site. 

Moreover, as of the end of March 2026, bidding opportunities for the project’s Phase II construction have just been opened yet some 50 million pesos have already been allocated for its Phase III, thus becoming a major point of concern for some students.

Rafael Jay Valix, former vice president of the TSU Supreme Student Council (SSC), and his party Sandigan TSU were the first to criticize the discrepancy between the project’s physical phase progress and its budget allocation in a video calling for transparency and accountability in terms of how the university utilizes its 2026 budget amounting to more than 1 billion pesos.

“Sa harap ng mahigit ₱1,036,714,000 na kabuuang budget ng unibersidad ngayong 2026, nananatiling maraming tanong ang walang malinaw na sagot... Bakit hindi natatapos ang mga proyekto gayong aprubado ang mga budget nito?” they shared in the post’s caption.

Student coalitions, such as the Alliance of Concerned Students - TSU and Kabataang Tarlakenyo para sa Bayan (KTB), who partook in the First Day Rage staged at the TSU Main Gate on July 21 echoed a similar sentiment, highlighting that the budget for the construction of the project’s third phase has been approved yet its physical framework remains in a “skeletal structure,” raising suspicions regarding transparency and accountability.

𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘆𝘀, 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗧𝗦𝗨’𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 

In an exclusive interview, however, the TSU Office of Facilities Development and Management (OFDM), clarified the real progress of the project, saying that as of July 12, 2025, the first phase has been completed under the control of DPWH RO3 as the implementing agency with RD8 Builders Corporation as the contractor, and will now proceed to the next phase.

Based on OFDM’s summary of events, the construction started as early as February 2024 but Phase I was just completed more or less a year after as the Notice to Proceed (NTP) had just been secured on January 13, 2025, seven months after the project was transferred to the DPWH pursuant to the Joint Memorandum Circular No. 01, s. 2024 of the department and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED).

Under such a joint memo, infrastructure projects of state universities and colleges (SUCs) exceeding 5 million pesos funded under the General Appropriations Act (GAA) are directly released to and implemented by regional DPWH offices.

With numerous SUCs in Central Luzon having infrastructure projects exceeding 5 million pesos, the DPWH RO3 was said to have been “overwhelmed”, stalling the issuance of the NTP and, more importantly, the construction of the dorm’s Phase I.

Amidst completing the first phase, the DPWH relinquished the power to implement the project back to the OFDM. 

However, even after giving the project back to the OFDM, delays in the construction persisted due to DPWH’s lapses in securing a building permit, an official written approval granted by a local government agency essential for one to start building, changing, or fixing a structure.

“Kaya lang, nagkaroon nga ng technical delays sa pag-process ng building permit. Nitong July 2026 pa lang nabigay sa amin ‘yung building permit. Date issued sa DPWH June 23, nabigay sa amin July 8,” the OFDM stated. 

“From January 2025 to July 2026, dun pa lang nabigay sa amin ‘yung building permit, dun pa lang na-complete lahat ng deliverables for the project. Hindi kasi kami pwedeng mag-proceed sa construction ng Phase II without the building permit,” the office stressed. 

As of press time, the procurement process for the construction of Phase II has been completed and the university will soon enter into a contract with the winning contractor once the Board of Regents (BOR) approves it. 

“Nakumpleto na lahat nung specified scope of work para sa Phase I. Ngayon ang magtutuloy na ay ang TSU kasi nakita na mabagal ang DPWH, na-overwhelm daw sila,” the OFDM added.

‘𝗡𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝘂𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻’

Meanwhile, in response to those who have raised concerns over the discrepancies between the budget and the project’s real progress, the office encouraged them to verify information first as allocating a budget for the project’s third phase does not necessarily mean it is already in that phase.

The office also emphasized that there is “no corruption” involved in the project, saying: “Hindi sumasawsaw ‘yung kamay namin sa pera, sa pondo ng project. Hindi siya iniipit ng office namin, ng administration. May public procurement, kami lang ang nag-e-evaluate,” it noted.

Now that the office, as TSU’s implementing arm, holds the control to continue the project, it projects that Phase II may be finished by next year around March or April, while it sets 2028 as the target year for the completion of Phase III and its opening for students and employees.

Furthermore, the office stated that it is making its efforts to commence the construction of the male dormitory.

“Hindi na hihintayin na matapos ‘yung female dorm bago simulan ‘yung male dorm. Magiging simultaneous siya kasi kailangan nating mag-comply sa batas na nagsasabing dapat may dorm ang mga SUCs,” it stated.

title: When-dy Mountain Calls: How One Ofw’s Grief Reached Tarlac’s Highest Peaks
author: Kate Aira L. Mendoza
excerpt: Her soul is at peak purpose; what’s keeping yours in the lowlands? For her, touching the sky meant reaching out to the indigenous Ayta communities who call these summits home.
body:
Her soul is at peak purpose; what’s keeping yours in the lowlands?

For her, touching the sky meant reaching out to the indigenous Ayta communities who call these summits home. In those cloud-draped villages, climbing closer to heaven became an act of devotion, providing support, warm meals, and outreach all in the name of grace and goodness.

𝗡𝗢 𝗧𝗜𝗖𝗞𝗘𝗧 𝗧𝗢 𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗘 

This was the very heart for others that defined Wendy Doll Lusong Arocena, 33, a woman who lived with faith and service.

In Dubai, she serves in the CFC - Singles for Christ community, guides children as a Kids for Christ Rock Leader, and handcrafts free rosaries through the Child of Mary ministry. As a United Arab Emirates Volunteer (Sharjah Base), she provided hands-on disaster relief during the Turkey-Syria earthquake.

She also runs the digital page SELF_1, creating uplifting content to evangelize and guide people of all ages. This deep-rooted compassion sparked the “Share Your Blessing” UAE Mission during the pandemic, mobilizing her family and Singles for Christ community to provide vital relief to struggling Filipinos and disaster victims back home.

However, across four thousand miles of silent sky and locked borders, Wendy’s father, Papa Edwin, had closed his eyes for the last time. At this moment, the world was paralyzed by pandemic restrictions, trapped behind mandatory quarantine walls and grounded flights.

For her, who had spent twelve long years pouring her youth into Taiwan and the Middle East so her family could eat three warm meals a day, the distance became a vast, impassable sea.

No final words escaped her lips. No flight brought her back to shore in time.

And when grief has no shore to land on, it turns inward, surging like an untamed tide. It craves a space where the crushing ache of loss can be surrendered to a higher power and transformed into something enduring. 

“I decided to surrender my heart to God,” Wendy recalls.

In that surrender, she set her compass toward a single vow: the moment the borders reopened and she could touch home soil, she would head straight for the mountains.

It was there, in the wake of an unsaid goodbye, that she would look to the sky, searching for a sign that the one she lost was still within reach.

𝗖𝗔𝗥𝗥𝗬𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗛𝗢𝗣𝗘 𝗨𝗣 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗟𝗢𝗣𝗘

Guided by what she felt was God’s hand, Wendy met a fellow devout in Dubai who also climbs with a mission to help the Ayta community, which opened a door for her into a world tucked high above the clouds—a world defined by rich culture, but shadowed by severe, systemic neglect. 

She did not care which peak stood before her, only that the trail was steep enough for the burning in her legs to steady the tempest in her chest. She wanted to climb until her boots were caked in soil and her lungs gasped for air, searching for a horizon wide enough to hold the  emptiness left in her father’s wake.

When the skies finally opened, she kept her promise to God and to herself. Pushing her body up rugged slopes, feeling the strain of every step, something shifted. 

The mountain didn’t erase her loss, but the height gave her a divine perspective.

The scripture from Matthew 25:40 whispered to her heart: “𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘪𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘣𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘦, 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘥𝘪𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘮𝘦.”

It was along these same mist-shrouded trails that her sinking feeling met a higher purpose.

Hearing of the hardships endured by indigenous families living in isolated mountain 𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘴, the fog of her personal pain began to clear. 
She realized her trek up the mountain was no longer just about burning off her own sorrow; it was answering a divine calling to carry hope to those who felt forgotten by the world below.

What began as a personal mission blossomed into a collective movement of compassion. The outreach effort, “Akyat Para Kay Kulot,” started with a tight circle of a dozen volunteers and quickly swelled into a family of nearly forty souls bound by a single cause: to carry light into the mountain's most forgotten corners.

This mission was fueled by a circle of sponsors—a community built from her own relatives, friends, kabarangays, and her second family in the CFC-SFC Dubai community, all uniting to send blessings from afar.

Their footsteps led them deep into the hinterlands, including the remote mountain community of Pampanga, and surrounding ancestral domains spanning Tarlac.

There were no paved roads here, nothing to ease the burden. To reach the families above, Wendy and her team carried everything on their backs, climbing on foot for over an hour up steep, unforgiving trails where no vehicle could ever venture.

Her heart bled for the young ones growing up in the shadows of those peaks.

High above the lowlands, where paved roads end and ambulances cannot reach, Wendy confronted a heartbreaking reality: over 80% of the remote upland 𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘴 across these ranges remain entirely cut off from basic needs. Being tucked away on these heights, indigenous households endure poverty rates nearly double the national average—isolated not just by height, but by systemic downfall.

There, Wendy watched elderly mothers and fathers, their faces weathered by decades of relentless sun, still breaking their backs over the soil just to scrape together a single meal.

Having spent a lifetime tilling land without access to education, many carried high rates of functional illiteracy, unable to read or write. Yet, pouring every drop of their remaining strength into their children’s survival, a living, breathing echo of her own father’s sacrificial heart.

𝗛𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘁-𝘀𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘀, 𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗮 𝗽𝗶𝗲𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗵.

𝗖𝗟𝗜𝗠𝗕 𝗖𝗟𝗢𝗦𝗘𝗥 𝗧𝗢 𝗛𝗘𝗔𝗩𝗘𝗡

Truly, the mountain does not heal a broken heart by erasing the pain, but by giving it a view wide enough to see beyond itself.

“𝗜’𝗺 𝗽𝗿𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗼𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝗮 𝗸𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗻 𝗻𝗶𝗹𝗮 𝗮𝘁 𝗻𝗴 𝗸𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗹𝘆𝗮. 𝗗𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻 𝗸𝗼 𝗿𝗶𝗻 𝗻𝗮 𝘀𝗮𝗻𝗮 𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗸𝗮𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗮 𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗮𝗽𝗮 𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘀𝗮𝘆𝗮𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝘂𝗵𝗮𝘆,” she shares. 

𝗔𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲-𝗮-𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝘣𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘬-𝘣𝘢𝘺𝘢𝘯 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴-𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗻.

Gratitude reminds us to cherish the fragile gifts we hold, while compassion calls us to step beyond ourselves and become a beacon of hope for those who have less. By living as a light for others in a struggling world, we build the greatest legacy possible, one woven from goodness, faith, and love that inspires generations to come.

Yet, her message is not a call for everyone to pack a bag and scale physical mountains. It is a reminder that every life holds the potential for grace, right where it stands.

For her, the vast, impassable sea that once separated her from home has finally found its shore.

Her father’s memory no longer lives in the silence of a missed farewell or the grief of locked borders. It lives in every supply pack carried up a muddy trail, in every warm smile shared with a child in the hills of Pampanga and Tarlac, and in the courageous beat of a daughter’s heart that chose to surrender her deepest pain to God and turn it into a lifelong journey of hope.

Through every steep ascent and every life touched along the ridge, the unspoken goodbye has finally found its voice—whispering across Tarlac’s highest peaks that love and faith, when given away, are never truly lost.

𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱𝘀, 𝘀𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗹𝗹.

title: ‘Tuloy ang laban naming katutubo!’: Capas residents, IPs mobilize against PAF’s stringent measures
author: Clarisse T. Fajardo
excerpt: Residents, farmers, and indigenous peoples (IPs) from barangays Bueno, Maruglo, O’Donnell, Sta. Lucia, and Sta. Juliana of Capas, Tarlac protested against the growing stringent measures and harassment of the Philippine Air Force (PAF) at Sitio Calanat, Barangay O’Donnell, July 14
body:
Residents, farmers, and indigenous peoples (IPs) from barangays Bueno, Maruglo, O’Donnell, Sta. Lucia, and Sta. Juliana of Capas, Tarlac protested against the growing stringent measures and harassment of the Philippine Air Force (PAF) at Sitio Calanat, Barangay O’Donnell, July 14.

The protest, which started at 5:00 AM and ran until 12 noon, marks the first mass mobilization collectively initiated by the five barangays.

Currently, there are three checkpoints headquartered at the Colonel Ernesto Rabina Air Base (CERAB) where these barangays are situated. 
Protocol has always been strict since 2016, especially when it came to who and what would be entering these premises because of the “No Permit, No Entry” policy. However, through the years, measures have escalated to the extent that the livelihood of the people has been disrupted, prompting affected communities to stage the mass action.

“Nagbebenta kami ng mga tinatanim namin na luya at saging, ‘yun ang hinaharang…kami kawawa. Saan kami kukuha [ng] panghanapbuhay namin? At kung gusto namin bumili ng kahit ano para sa bahay namin e hinaharang,” Burot Ocampo, a tribal chieftain from Barangay Sta. Juliana, echoed what residents experienced. 

𝗣𝗔𝗙'𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

According to community members, PAF officers would also regularly visit people’s homes to ensure no form of construction or renovation was done. If there were, evidence would be taken and sent to file a report at the barangay office. 

“Kunware nagpatayo ka ng CR (comfort room) o gripo, pupunta roon. Pagkatapos bibidyohan saka ipapa-blotter sa barangay,” a resident from Bueno said. 

Materials needed for the renovation of homes, including cement, plywood, steel, metal roofing, and more, were prohibited from proceeding past the first checkpoint according to the PAF’s protocol. Moreover, rice, water, and farming equipment, such as tractors were also banned. 

One resident explained that even cement needed for tombs was thoroughly checked as PAF officers verify the authenticity of these deaths. Permits are also needed before allowing materials to be brought in.

“Pati bahay ng patay, hinaharang na,” they stated. 

However, even when permits were requested, approval from their head takes from one week to a month. 

“Kailangan daw ng permit sa itaas. Kaso naman, hindi na naman pipirmahan [ang] permit na ipapasa mo roon. Hindi rin gagawin. Parang matetengga na lang ‘yung materyales mo,” a resident from Maruglo shared. 

Alex Vitug, a tribal chieftain from Bueno, asserted that they did not want things to escalate this way but the strict protocol has made living harder for the people. 

“Ayaw sana namin makipag-away. Ngayon kasi, sobra na pong higpit sa amin! Sana makisama sila! Dapat nakikinig din sila,” he stated. 

𝗟𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗼𝗳 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 

National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) - Tarlac representative Gilbert Cuero clarified that this is not the first protest the residents have done. A peace rally was staged before by the residents of Sta. Juliana. However, this was the first protest where almost 3,000 people from five barangays of Capas, Tarlac mobilized together.

Moreover, this case has already reached Raffy Tulfo, a politician and media personality best known for solving disputes in his show Raffy Tulfo in Action (RTIA) in 2015. It has been 11 years since then. 

According to Cuero, paperwork was submitted to different organizations of the government, including the Air Force Real Estate Office (AFREO), but the issue remained stagnant. 

“Ilang sulat na ang ginawa natin, ilang presidente na sinulatan natin, kumpleto ako sa sulat,” he asserted. 

Cuero also explained that in the response letter of AFREO, it stated that the stringent protocol was for the sake of the IPs. 

“Nilagay niya sa sulat na nanghaharang ng mga materyales para sa kapakanan ng katutubo, hindi ‘yung ganiyan. Walang binanggit na mga farm lots, mga bahay na binabawal na lahat,” he said.

𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜𝗣 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 

Besides the restriction of materials, with most villagers from Sta. Juliana being IPs, farmers were prone to having their land taken with no due process, compensation, or Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC).

“Pagkuha ng mga lupain ng mga farmers nang hindi sila dumadaan sa tamang proseso, walang bayad. At the same time, pagputol ng mga kahoy ng mga residente na pinagbibintangan pa ‘yung mga residente na pumutol e sila mismong Air Force [ang] pumutol kasi nga maano sila sa DENR,” he said. 

“Mas masaklap kami diyan kasi nandito gate nila so kami pinaka number one [na] affected diyan, Barangay Sta. Juliana tsaka Bueno,” he added.

Moreover, Cuero questioned the assertion of Republic Act No. 8371, or the “Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act (IPRA) of 1997” saying: “Nandiyan ang RA 8371 na mangangalaga sana sa kapakanan ng mga katutubo. Bakit hanggang munisipyo namomroblema sila ngayon?”

The IPs also asserted that their ancestors had lived within the area even before the eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991, yet, were still pressured to leave as PAF declared the premises as a “Danger Zone” where their Military Reservation Camps are located and Balikatan Exercises are done. 

As such, residents protested against Republic Act No. 7227, or “The Bases Conversion and Development Act of 1992”, and Proclamation No. 163, or the designation and transfer of lands pursuant to R.A. 7227.

“Kaya nagkaisa na itong limang barangay para kundinahin ang maling pamamalakad nitong Air Force,” Cuero emphasized. 

𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘂𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗣𝗔𝗙

“Ayun po sana hinihiling namin sa Philippine Air Force, makipagdiyalogo sa amin para magkaroon ng maayos na patakaran na susundin, na magkakaayos po ang aming munisipyo, ang aming kababayan atsaka po ang Philippine Air Force para hindi po nagkakaganito,” Capas Mayor Hon. Roseller "Boots" Rodriguez, who appeared amidst the demonstration, said. 

The mayor admitted to having feelings of helplessness as PAF's protocol are rules that their office cannot bypass. He encouraged, however, the Air Force to acknowledge the presence of IPs in the area years before their office was headquartered here. 

“Kilalanin po ‘yung kasalukuyang na pagokupa ng aming kababayan na nandito sa loob ng Military Reservation dahil mas nauna pa po sila kaysa sa pagdating po ng Air Force dito sa aming lugar,” he said. 

In a post by PTV, PAF Spokesperson Col. Ma. Christina Basco acknowledged the raised concerns from yesterday’s protest, but remained firm that the premises are still a danger zone. 

“Doon po kasi natin kino-conduct ’yung ating live fire exercises. ‘Yung mga kababayan natin, it’s unsafe basically for them kaya nga pinapakiusapan na kapag mayroong live fire exercises ay i-clear ang area. Medyo may challenge na minsan paalisin sila, pero patuloy natin silang sinasabihan to clear the area for their safety,” Basco stated. 

Basco assured that the PAF has coordinated with the local government units, the National Housing Authority (NHA), National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), human rights and land management authorities, and other concerned offices and agencies regarding this issue.

title: CCS, COS valedictorians call for systemic reform, public service as TSU closes week-long 2026 grad rites
author: Nicolle C. Garcia
excerpt: Tarlac State University (TSU) officially concluded its week-long 37th Commencement Exercises on July 31 at the University Gymnasium, capping off four days of graduation ceremonies with the conferment of degrees to its final two student…
body:
Tarlac State University (TSU) officially concluded its week-long 37th Commencement Exercises on July 31 at the University Gymnasium, capping off four days of graduation ceremonies with the conferment of degrees to its final two student batches.

The morning session celebrated 559 graduates from the College of Industrial Technology (CIT) and College of Computer Science (CCS), while the final afternoon session honored 586 graduates from the College of Science (COS) and College of Criminal Justice Education (CCJE).

Taking the stage during the morning session, class valedictorian Aron Jez Arboleda, magna cum laude from the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science shared that he entered college simply to learn and follow his heart, but pursuing his passions ultimately exposed a troubling reality facing his generation.

“Nasa punto na ba tayo na wala ng kalayaang pumili ang mga kabataan para sa kanilang hinaharap? Na kailangan laging maging praktikal at piliin ang mga kursong na kayang bumuhay, kahit na hindi ito ang gusto?” Arboleda asked.

He pointed out that hidden issues like poverty, pressure, high educational costs, and breadwinner expectations keep youth in survival mode, depriving many Filipinos of the freedom to pursue their true interests.

“Kaya patuloy po akong nangangarap, hindi para sa mataas na grado, kundi para sa Pilipinas na kayang magbigay ng balikat sa kaniyang mga tao. Kaya sa pagpapatuloy, huwag nating nila-’lang’ ang edukasyon,” he added.

Recounting his experience with an organization teaching indigenous Aeta children, Arboleda noted that even 50 to 60-year-olds express a desire to study, illustrating how marginalized communities are often deprived of basic education.

“Kung sino pa po ang nagpapanatili ng gintong kultura ng ating bansa, ay sila pa po ang nangunguna sa ating marginalized sectors. Let’s not take things for granted. Hugutin at hanapin natin ang rason kung bakit natin ginagawa ang mga ito. Para saan, at para kanino,” Arboleda emphasized.

While in the afternoon session, class valedictorian Vhon Andre Alvero, summa cum laude, from BS Environmental Science, challenged the notion of “free” higher education, sharing the financial hardships that students endure just to attend classes daily. 

“Hindi libre ang mag-aral sa Tarlac State University. Hindi tunay na libre ang edukasyon sa TSU,” Alvero declared. “Hindi natin masisisi ang mga estudyante na mas pinipiling lumiban sa klase para makapagtrabaho.”

He also stressed that being state scholars entails a profound duty to give back to the taxpayers whose sweat, blood, and taxes funded their privilege.

“Gaya ng panata ng TSU, pagsumikapin nating hanapin ang katotohanan, magsilbi sa taong bayan, at pagbukludin ang bawat isa para sa ikauunlad ng bansa. Tandaan, ang bigat ng diploma at medalya at hindi nasusukat sa materyal nito, kundi sa kaakibat na responsibilidad kung paano natin gagamitin ang talino, lakas, husay, at talino upang ipaglaban at iangat ang mga nasa laylayan,” Alvero challenged the graduates.

On the other hand, CCS’s Arboleda reminded his fellow graduates of their shared duty to build a nation rooted in empathy and accountability.

"I have faith in us. Nakita ko ang pagsisikap at pagpupursigi ng aking mga kapwa mag aaral nitong apat na taon," Arboleda stated, closing the commencement season on a hopeful note.

title: PBBM vows to return stolen funds by kleptocrats to Filipinos, lays out new plans in SONA ‘26
author: Andrei P. Opeña
excerpt: After blasting corrupt individuals involved in the flood control schemes “shame on you” and vowing to jail them all in 2025, triggering a government-wide investigation, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.
body:
After blasting corrupt individuals involved in the flood control schemes “shame on you” and vowing to jail them all in 2025, triggering a government-wide investigation, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has promised to return the ill-gotten assets recovered from corrupt officials back to the Filipino people.

“Ang pondo na naisalba natin na balak ibulsa ng mga tiwaling opisyal ay sa taumbayan natin ibubuhos,” Marcos pledged before a jam-packed Batasang Pambansa Complex in Quezon City on July 27 as he delivered his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA).

Since launching the investigation, Marcos bared that over 20 billion pesos have been recovered, 800 million pesos of which have been remitted to the treasury.

He also noted that various contractors, high-ranking officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), and even legislators have been charged and imprisoned.

In light of this, the chief executive said that he plans to provide more support for most Filipinos in need as the hefty effects of the conflict in the Middle East continue to be felt in the country, as reflected in the surging prices of oil, fuel, and other essential products, to which Marcos claimed the government “did everything possible” to ease.

“Ngayon, ipipihit natin ang mga programa sa mas nangangailangan nating kapwa-Pilipino, para naman mas malawak at mas marami ang maaabot ng tulong,” he stated.

Besides these, Marcos has laid out new commitments as he enters the final stretch of his term, focusing primarily on the amendments to policies involving tax, electricity, and the long-standing geopolitical dispute over the West Philippine Sea.

On electricity, Marcos called on Filipino legislators to scrap the system loss charges, saying they must not be charged to the electricity bills of consumers.

"Pinapasa ito sa konsyumer at kinakarga sa bill na pinapatungan pa ng value-added tax. Hindi naman kasalanan ng konsyumer kung bakit nagkaroon ng systems loss. Kaya hindi naman tama na kailangan sila pa ang pagbabayarin dito," Marcos remarked.

In line with this, Marcos urged the immediate amendment of the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) enacted in 2001 to lower electricity prices through competition and power sector reforms, as well as the passage of a “Sariling Kuryente Act” that would make installing rooftop solar power systems easier.

"Therefore, we, the people request–no, we demand for the immediate amendment of the EPIRA and to prohibit charging systems loss against consumers including the value-added tax thereon,” he said.

In terms of tax, Marcos aims to recalibrate the country’s income tax bracket, pressing the Congress to raise the minimum annual tax exemption threshold from 250,000 to 350,000 pesos, while exempting small businesses from minimum corporate tax, and granting a broad tax amnesty.

“[W]e will pursue tax relief measures that promote growth, generate revenue, and advance equity toward socio-economic sustainability,” he stated.

Meanwhile, following the depiction of a Chinese state-run publication of the Filipinos as monkeys in criticizing the 2016 Arbitral award, Marcos reminded “our friends and our detractors” that Filipinos are “not greedy, not racist, and not liars.”

More importantly, he strongly reaffirmed the country’s sovereign rights in the WPS, vowing to use peaceful and legal means to defend its territory, stating “We are Filipinos and we do not yield.”

“Your government will do all that is necessary to continue upholding this Award, utilizing every peaceful and legal means available to the Republic against any attempt, foreign or domestic, to undermine this achievement,” he added. 

Moreover, the president also outlined various other promises aimed at benefiting other sectors. On transportation, he assured Filipinos that the North-South Commuter Railway and Metro Rail Transit Line 7 (MRT-7) will be operational by 2027. 

He also announced his target that by 2040, half of all vehicles on Philippine roads are electric-powered, thus mandating the government to support modernization and prioritize electric vehicles (EVs) in fleet upgrades.

In addition, amidst growing public criticism, Marcos touted the US-led initiative Pax Silica, which will turn some 1,620-hectare site in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac into an artificial intelligence (AI) processing hub. He emphasized that it is part of the country’s cause for “bigger and greater things” by “venturing into areas heretofore unimaginable.”

In relation to the Philippines being prone to various disasters and calamities that have led to severe human, material, economic, and environmental losses, Marcos promised the construction of disaster-resilient “Ligtas Pinoy Centers.” This project will primarily be built in areas frequently affected by severe weather conditions, including Bicol, Eastern Samar, Bukidnon, and Davao de Oro.

“Ang lahat ng gusali sa ating bansa ay dapat handa, at kayang manatiling matatag at nakatindig laban sa anumang banta ng sakuna at kalamidad,” Marcos shared.

With this, he called for amendments to the National Building Code as he aims to align the country’s construction requirements with modern standards.

Furthermore, in terms of health, Marcos announced the expansion of the Philhealth preventive health program in 2027 by gradually including blood tests and medicines aimed at detecting and monitoring kidney, liver, and thyroid conditions, as well as hepatitis B.

He also vowed to complete the distribution of land titles to beneficiaries of agrarian reform by next year and the cancellation of their debts. 

To the victims of the tragic shooting in Tacloban City, he recognized them for their “unflinching and heroic virtue,” thereby urging for stronger protection of children from violence and harmful influences.

But amidst his fifth SONA becoming his longest, having been delivered for 1 hour and 26 minutes, various pressing issues were unaddressed, including the ongoing militarization efforts of the Philippine National Police (PNP) and the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), as well as the crimes against humanity and impeachment trials of the former president Rodrigo Duterte and incumbent Vice President Sara Duterte, respectively.

Moreover, Marcos also failed to give an update on the progress of the “missing sabungeros’ case, as well as the manhunt for Atong Ang, former Ako Bicol partylist Rep. Zaldy Co, and Sen. Ronald “Bato” de la Rosa, who all continue to refuse to face the public and evade accountability.

title: National Campus Press Freedom Day
author: Janeth G. Gamboa
excerpt: I have an ID idly sitting on my desk. Not like the common ones. Laminated, worn at the corners where the plastic has begun to turn into a cloudy cataract obscuring the photo underneath.
body:
I have an ID idly sitting on my desk.

Not like the common ones. Laminated, worn at the corners where the plastic has begun to turn into a cloudy cataract obscuring the photo underneath. The photo on the card — well me, in the light of what I think was a Monday morning. Beneath the photo, in large capital letters:

𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗦.

I like to pick it up sometimes. Not to wear it, just to hold it. To feel the weight of something that is supposed to be light. A card — plastic and yet, it feels heavier than it is letting on.

I put it down. I pick it up again. Then put it down again. Time and time again, I am still learning what it means to carry it.

When the announcement about the National Higher Education Press Conference (NHEPC) broke, my phone lit up with dozens of messages.

“𝘕𝘚𝘗𝘊 𝘵𝘰 𝘕𝘏𝘌𝘗𝘊, 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘮 𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘯!”

“𝘉𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘵𝘰 𝘝𝘪𝘨𝘢𝘯!”

“𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦𝘴 𝘮𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘫𝘰𝘪𝘯 𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘸.”

And I too share their excitement. The National Higher Education Press Conference. First-ever. Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao — all sharing the center stage. Not gonna lie, there is something genuinely enchanting about that idea.

But there is always a flaw in the system.

I have seen what happens when press conferences become the publication’s entire reason for existing. School publication going radio silent and then reappearing the moment press conference season starts thawing.

“𝘐 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘢𝘯 𝘙𝘚𝘗𝘊 𝘘𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘳,” they say, when medals and achievements are not the currency for entering a college publication. When competition starts being their highlight — as if the work for the newspaper is just a mere backdrop for the competition season they actually signed up for.

It is such a big slap to what collegiate journalism has been built upon — not of contest journalism but of pure service for the people.

Let us not have contest journalism culture bleed upward. From the NSPC dreams system, where young journalists focus their hearts on training to stand upon the highest podium and not for the stories itself. Now with the NHEPC, I am afraid — genuinely, deeply afraid — that we are about to import that culture into collegiate journalism, where the stakes are higher and the mandate is heavier.

Especially in these times where parts of the nation are still lagging behind press freedom. And I do not think of it as a mere accident — but a symptom.

For instance, Mindanao belongs to those who have never been gentle with the press. It is the region where journalists have been silenced not just by indifference but by something far more deliberate. So a dream for NHEPC is also a dream for the regional level of the south-most Philippines.

I think about this as I stare at my press ID. I think about what it means to be carrying it in a collegiate setting — in a place where the administration is not always our ally, where immersing too hard on a story can make you feel the weight of the eyes on your back.

NHEPC is a platform. A good one, even. A stage where journalists can share their crafts and find each other across islands — and there is nothing wrong with wanting that.

But a platform is only as meaningful as the stories it brings forth with it. To being involved in the heart of the news — to the high and lows when immersing with the masses.

I am not saying competitions are bad. I refuse to settle for that easy conclusion. For many of us, press conferences were the first time we understood that maybe the words we piece together could mean something. It is part of the foundation that gifted us passion for journalism. A medal is not a virus. It becomes one when the medal becomes the only reason you bleed the pen — and when you put the pen down the moment no medals are waiting.

We can hold both truths at once.

I picked up the Press ID again, resting it around my neck. Time to set out and interview about stories needed to be told. No one asked me to do it. No one asked me to write it. There will be no stage, no recognition, and no applause when I tell the tale of their lives.

𝘼𝙣𝙙 𝙩𝙝𝙖𝙩’𝙨 𝙤𝙠𝙖𝙮. 𝙄 𝙬𝙞𝙡𝙡 𝙬𝙧𝙞𝙩𝙚 𝙖𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙞𝙩 𝙖𝙣𝙮𝙬𝙖𝙮. 𝘽𝙚𝙘𝙖𝙪𝙨𝙚 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙨 𝙞𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙬𝙚𝙞𝙜𝙝𝙩 𝙤𝙛 𝙖 𝙋𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙨 𝙄𝘿.

It is not bad to set your goals out for the nationals, but I hope this will not be the only reason why we are joining a publication — especially in this bloodbath and bludgeoning.

title: TSU studes snag title in 4th Refugee Film Fest Short Film Comp
author: Vincent Jayne B. Pallasigui
excerpt: Tarlac State University’s (TSU) entry to the 4th Refugee Film Festival secured the championship title in the short film category during the awarding ceremony held at the Natividad Fajardo-Rosario Gonzalez Auditorium of De La Salle…
body:
Tarlac State University’s (TSU) entry to the 4th Refugee Film Festival secured the championship title in the short film category during the awarding ceremony held at the Natividad Fajardo-Rosario Gonzalez Auditorium of De La Salle University, June 20.

Produced by TSU students Kharl Angelo Manaloto, Kissy Pingol, and Angel Gabrielle Rico under the TR3S Production, the entry titled “Tambol” revolves around the story of Ikil, a 19-year-old Badjao facing forced displacement, discrimination, and staleness in the city.

In an interview, Manaloto, the short film’s director, shared their journey in making the film, highlighting the complex roles they have to play and the things they went through to produce an award-winning entry. 

“Our team was composed of three people, kaya everything, from acting and writing, kami-kami lang. Sobrang complex ng mga roles namin sa pelikulang ito,” he shared.

“At first, I was unmotivated. I wanted to back out kasi tinatamad talaga ako and I was doubting my skills. Pero pumasok sa isip ko na, ‘the biggest loss you will have is not trying’,” he added.

More than the recognition, Manaloto emphasized the core message that the short film wants to convey.

“We wanted to show everyone that badjaos also want to own properties, have work opportunities, and be free from discrimination. We often see them begging, but why are they begging? It’s because of discrimination,” he noted.

With the award, Manaloto expressed his desire to direct his next film in the future with the aim of delivering a profound message to a broader audience.

“As of now, we are aiming to join more film contests to showcase our work and deliver a message that no one has seen before,” he stated.
The Work congratulates the TR3S Production for bringing home pride and honor. May you continue to use your platform to uphold the voices that deserve to be heard.

title: Agawang-lupa sa mga katutubo, inalmahan ng lokal na simbahan, mga progresibong grupo; mga residente, nagpahayag ng agam-agam
author: Renz Joshua D.T. De Vera
excerpt: Inilarawan ng mga lider ng independent churches, mga kabataan, at ng mga pinunong lokal bilang 'di makatwirang panghihimasok sa mga sagradong lupa ng mga ninuno ang pagpapatag sa mga sakahan ng Sitio Binyanyan, at mga karatig sitio nito.
body:
Inilarawan ng mga lider ng independent churches, mga kabataan, at ng mga pinunong lokal bilang 'di makatwirang panghihimasok sa mga sagradong lupa ng mga ninuno ang pagpapatag sa mga sakahan ng Sitio Binyanyan, at mga karatig sitio nito.

Ito ang naging sentro ng iba't-ibang mga hinain ng mga residente sa isinagawang Indigenous People's Celebration, sa ilalim ng open consultation sa mga katutubo, nitong Agosto 11.

Kabilang sa pagtitipon ang mga kawani mula sa mga sitiong maaapektuhan sa pagpapatayo ng Pax Silica Hub. Pinangunahan ng mga lider mula sa iba't-ibang sektor ang talakayan hinggil sa mga mayoryang problema tungkol sa kalikasan at inobasyon.

Sa mga ipinahayag na solidarity call, nanawagan ang mga katutubong lider na pagkakaisa ang magiging laban nila sa lumalagong agresyon at tensyon ng mga agawang-lupa.

“Mga kasama na magsasaka na apektado ng isyu, dapat ay magsama-sama tayo sa pagtutol sa Pax Silica. Ang pag-unlad ay dapat para sa karamihan at hindi para sa iilan lamang,” sambit ni Mang Nel, representante ng mga magsasaka.

Nilinaw ng mga residente na ang lupang katutubo ay ipinamana sa kanila ng mga ninuno. Ito ay matapos maapektuhan ang dating komunidad ng mga Aeta sa pagputok ng Mt. Pinatubo. Dito na raw sila lumaki nang mahabang panahon pagkaraan ng insidente, at nabubuhay na sila ngayon sa yaman ng lupa.

“Itinaboy na nga kami ng Mt. pinatubo, itataboy pa ng Pax Silica. Sa lupa kami nabuhay. Kung itataboy kami dito, paano pa kami mabubuhay?,” pahayag ni Ka Anton, isang katutubong lider.

Bukod sa mga pagpapatag sa Sitio Binyanyan, umaakyat na rin ang mga kuro-kuro at pag-aalala hinggil sa mababang pagbili ng lupa sa mga karatig na komunidad, partikular sa Sitio Kalangitan. 

Ang hinain ng mga lokal na nakatira roon ay ang patuloy nilang panawagan at saloobin sa pagprotekta ng kanilang sagrado na lupa. 
“Tayo po ay nasa Diyos. Dahil po pinagpala tayo, lalaban tayo. Lahat ng katutubo, nagmamahal sa kalikasan. Kami ang tagapangalaga nito, hindi ang Pax Silica,” pahayag ni Ka Tess, kinatawan ng komunidad.

Sa kabilang banda, nilinaw ng Bases Conversion Development Authority (BCDA) na wala diumanong maapektuhan na komunidad o sasakuping ancestral land ang itatayong AI Data Center sa Capas, Tarlac. Magbibigay din daw ito ng oportunidad sa workforce ng lalawigan at magpapalakas ng economic stronghold ng bansa.

Mariin itong pinabulaanan ng mga organisasyong dumalo sa pagtitipon. Ang problemang kinakaharap ng mga katutubo sa pagpapatag ng pinaniniwalaang “early phasing” ng proyekto ay isa na raw malinaw na indikasyon na mayroong nangyayaring diskriminasyon sa mga kapatid na Aeta.

“Ito po ay hindi totoo. The fact na nakakaranas po ang mga kapatid nating katutubo ng agresyon ay contradicting o pagtutol mula mismo sa kanilang mga sinabi,” pagdiriin ni Mx. Aisa, isang representate mula sa mga progresibong grupo.

Ang Pax Silica ay isang US-led economic security initiative na nakatakdang maging isa sa pinakamalaking AI data center sa Pilipinas. Itatayo ang 1,600-ektaryang pasilidad sa New Clark City, kung saan maraming ancestral domains ang maaring maapektuhan.

Partikular sa isyu na kinakaharap ng pagpapatayo ng nasabing pasilidad ay ang mababang bayad sa titulo ng lupa, malabong plano para sa relokasyon ng mga katutubo, hindi malinaw na diskurso sa pagitan ng mga lokal na lider, at mismatched opportunities para sa mga maapektuhan nito.

Ngayong nakabinbin at walang konkretong direksyon ang mga usapin laban sa lupa-to-silica, mananatiling puno ng mga agam-agam, ang dating payapang lupa ng Sitio Kalangitan, at ng mga karatig-komunidad sa paanan nito.

title: Cine-tch Itey: Bakla, Kulayan mo ang Lente ng Mundo
author: Joshua Adrian N. Castro
excerpt: Lingid sa kaalaman ng karamihan, sa tiyan daw ang pinakamabilis na daan tungo sa kaibuturan ng isang lalang. Busugin ito. Lamnan.
body:
Lingid sa kaalaman ng karamihan, sa tiyan daw ang pinakamabilis na daan tungo sa kaibuturan ng isang lalang. Busugin ito. Lamnan. Kumbaga, h’wag mag-iiwan ng puwang sa kaniyang kaloob-looban. Pero, hindi alam ng iba, sa mata ang shortcut.

Kung puso lang din naman ang nais na maabot, ‘di sapat ang busog lang ito sa pag-ibig. Dapat, nakaiintindi rin. Na kapag tumagos sa paningin ang pag-ibig, dapat, lubos na unawa ng puso ang bawat gramo pagmamahal, maski katiting, maski hindi pangkaraniwan. At a kahit magpang-abot man sa kahit anong punto, palagi nitong pipiliing magpalaya.

Ito ang ihahain ng mga susunod na pelikulang bayan. Ihanda ang sarili. Buksan ang isipan, wakwakin kung maaari. Ating silipin ang iba’t ibang kulay ng pagmamahal gamit ang iisang lente ng kasarinlan.

𝐑𝐀𝐈𝐍𝐁𝐎𝐖’𝐒 𝐒𝐔𝐍𝐒𝐄𝐓

Isa sa mga tampok na pelikula ng 2018 Metro Manila Film Festival (MMFF), ang Rainbow’s Sunset handog ang kuwento nina Ramon at Fredo na pinatunayang kailanman ay hindi huli ang lahat para iladlad ang tunay na kulay ng bahaghari.

Hindi sinag ng araw ang sumalubong sa pag-iibigan nina Ramon at Fredo, kundi ang mapagkalingang titig ng buwan, mga nakaw na sulyap, at mga sandaling hindi kailangang ihayag. Ngunit kasabay sa takipsilim ang pag-agaw ng dilim sa makulay na buhay ni Fredo.

Isa sa mga makabagbag damdamin na tagpo ng pelikula ay ang pagkompronta ni Sylvia kay Fredo ukol sa lihim nila ni Ramon. Dito, sinambit ni Fredo ang mga katagang matagal nang nakaukit sa kaniyang puso: “Alam ko lugar ko. Alam kong mali. Alam kong bawal. Alam ko hindi ko na dapat siya ipaglaban.”

Sapagkat ayon sa lipunan, ito’y isang sakit—isang panandaliang yugto ng pagkalito sa sariling pagkakakilanlan. Kung ang sintomas ay ang pagbilis ng tibok ng puso, pagkapos ng hininga’t pagsikip ng dibdib tuwing kailangang magpanggap, ang tunay na karamdaman ay hindi ang kakayahan nilang magmahal. Ito ang malalang kanser ng pagtanggi at epidemyang bulag sa taglay na kulay ng bahaghari.

Ito ang pelikulang nagbibigay liwanag sa pananaw ng mga nakatatandang miyembro ng makulay na komunidad. Sa paglalakbay nina Ramon at Fredo, natagpuan nila ang yaman na mayroon sa dulo ng bahaghari. Hindi yari sa ginto, kundi galing sa puso. Isang pagmamahal u isinilang sa dilim, na ngayo’y malayang nakahihinga sa simoy ng gintong liwayway.

Sapagkat ang bahaghari sa kalangitan ay hindi kailanman maitatago. Gaano man kalakas ang ulan, darating ang oras na muli itong lilitaw—hindi lamang upang magbigay-kulay sa mundo, kundi upang ipaalala na ang bawat anyo ng pag-ibig ay nararapat makita.

𝐆𝐈𝐑𝐋, 𝐁𝐎𝐘, 𝐁𝐀𝐊𝐋𝐀, 𝐓𝐎𝐌𝐁𝐎𝐘

Sa unang tingin, ang pelikulang ito ay sumusunod sa komedyang Pilipino—maingay, mabilis ang mga tagpo upang humakot ng tawa sa takilya. Isa ito sa mga huling pelikulang binigyang buhay ni direktor Wenn V. Deramas kung saan ang wika ng pelikula ay isinasalin sa pamamagitan ng mga eksenang eksaherada na pinangungunahan ng komedyanteng si Vice Ganda.

Umiikot ang kuwento sa apat na magkakambal na pinaghiwalay ng tadhana at ng magkaibang estado sa buhay: sina Girlie, Peter, Mark Jill, at Panying. Nang magkasakit si Peter, napilitang mag-krus muli ang landas ng apat upang maghanap ng katugmang donor. Ngunit sa likod ng pilit na pag-aayos ng gusot sa kanilang pamilya, ang muling pagkikita ay nagdala rin ng komprontasyon sa pagitan ng kanilang mga pagkakaiba, kinalakihang mundo, at higit sa lahat—ang kanilang mga oryentasyon.

Tampok ng pelikula ang pagkakahati-hati. Sa pagbuo ng mga karakter na kumakatawan sa apat na kasarian, hinubog ng naratibo ang isang pira-pirasong salamin ng lipunang Pilipino.

Sa kultura na nakaugat pa rin sa relihiyosong doktrina at patriyarka, ang pagtatakda kung saan lamang pwedeng lumugar ay isang pang-araw-araw na pakikibaka. Ang bawat silid, bawat banyo, at bawat pampublikong lugar na ginagalawan ng mga karakter ay naging simbolo ng limitasyong ipinapataw ng lipunan.

Ngunit ang tunay na lakas ng pelikula ay hindi nagtatapos sa loob ng sinehan.

Dahil bago pa man hatulan at lagyan ng label ng isang mapanghusgang sistema ang katawan at pagkakakilanlan ng tao, ang pelikula ay nananatiling isang paalala: ang pag-iral ay hindi isang pagtatanghal, ito ay isang karapatan na walang sino man ang pwedeng humatol.

𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐊𝐈𝐄

Sa mundong ang pag-ibig ng mga kababaihan ay madalas ituring na bawal na laro, may mga pusong handang sumuway sa patakaran upang magwagi.

Higit pa sa kwentong palakasan, ang pelikulang Rookie (2023) ay sumasalamin sa karanasan ng mga kababaihang umibig sa kapwa babae. Isang naratibong patuloy na naiiba sa paningin ng marami, ngunit mga danas at dapat na may representasyon sa ating lipunan.

Naipinta ang obrang ito mula sa lente ng mga 𝘩𝘪𝘨𝘩 𝘴𝘤𝘩𝘰𝘰𝘭 𝘢𝘵𝘩𝘭𝘦𝘵𝘦 na sina Ace at Jana. Bilang 𝘵𝘦𝘢𝘮 𝘤𝘢𝘱𝘵𝘢𝘪𝘯 ng katunggali, malamig ang naging pagtanggap ni Jana kay Ace. Ngunit sa bawat ensayo, at bawat laban, ang distansiyang minsang namagitan sa kanila ay unti-unting napalitan ng mga sulyap, katahimikan, at mga damdaming hindi mapangalanan. Habang umaalingawngaw ang dagundong ng bawat palo ng bola, isang pag-ibig ang marahang sumabay sa ritmo ng laro—banayad, ngunit sapat upang baguhin ang takbo ng kanilang mga buhay.

Ngunit ang pinakamalakas na hampas ng pelikula ay wala sa tunggalian. Nang maranasan ni Ace ang panghihipo mula sa kanilang pisyoterapista, ang unang naging tugon niya ay ang nakasanayang kultura ng pag-aalinlangan: ang kumbinsihin ang sariling normal lamang ang marahas, ang piliing manahimik sa takot na walang makikinig.

Subalit sa sandaling ibinahagi niya ang bigat na ito kay Jana, ang kanilang umuusbong na romantikong ugnayan ay naging ligtas na kanlungan.

Sa bawat segundo ng pelikula ay naipipinta ang isang anyo ng pagmamahal na nararapat maranasan ng lahat—pagmamahal na hindi sumusukat sa kasarian, hindi nagpapataw ng takot, at hindi nagtatakda ng hangganan sa kung sino ang karapat-dapat mahalin. Sa pinakasimple nitong anyo, ipinapaalala ng pelikula na ang pag-ibig ay hindi kailanman dapat ikulong sa mga pamantayang itinakda ng lipunan, kundi hayaang umiral bilang isang puwersang mapagpalaya.

title: Comelec Tarlac City called out for allegedly “turning away” voter registration applicants on last day
author: Andrei P. Opeña
excerpt: Ken Austria, a law student and formerly a bemedalled power lifter from Tarlac State University (TSU), took to Facebook to air his frustration over the conduct of Comelec Tarlac City, specifically one of its election officers, during the…
body:
Ken Austria, a law student and formerly a bemedalled power lifter from Tarlac State University (TSU), took to Facebook to air his frustration over the conduct of Comelec Tarlac City, specifically one of its election officers, during the last day of nationwide voter registration today, May 18.

In his post, Austria shared that his brother, who was supposed to register as a voter, was allegedly turned away despite arriving at the registration center at a time still “well within operating hours.”

According to Austria, the election officer, who he said to have been Ruth Ellaine Dimarucot, refused to accommodate applicants due allegedly to “limited stubs” and “maximum capacity.”

“This is a direct violation of RA 8189 and COMELEC’s own resolution on Last Day Registration,” he stated.

Austria specified Sec. 8 of RA 8189, or the “Voter’s Registration Act”, and Sec. 6(b) of the COMELEC Resolution No. 11177, as two of the provisions of the regulations the officer violated. He argued, “My brother was there at 1:30 PM. Office hours run until 5:00 PM. There is no legal basis for refusal.”

He added that the officer’s conduct also constitutes a potential election offense under Sec. 45 (j) in relation to Sec. 8, which Sec. 46 of the law penalizes with imprisonment of not less than 1 year but not more than 6 years, disqualification from public office, and deprivation of the right of suffrage.

Additionally, they were questioned as to why they had only filed for registration now, to which Austria asserted that there is no provision in the law that requires a voter to register within a specific timeframe.

“My brother is now deprived of his right to vote in the BSKE through no fault of his own,” Austria lamented.

As of press time, there is no official statement released from the official Facebook page of Comelec Tarlac City.

title: Pax Parasitica: The Silicon Leech
body:
The history of the Philippines is a long study in parasitic extraction: foreign powers latching onto the archipelago, slowly feasting on our soil, power, and minerals while leaving the host diminished. Like any insidious infection, this systemic exploitation thrives in the shadows, dismissed as routine commerce or celebrated as development.

One of the latest manifestations of this dynamic comes packaged as Pax Silica—a US-driven initiative aiming to integrate the Philippines into the global semiconductor assembly chain. Official narratives paint a picture of mutual prosperity, celebrating economic zones like New Clark City as hubs of modern innovation. Yet, a closer look reveals that this "silica peace" is strictly one-sided.

By tethering our national resources to foreign strategic interests, the state surrenders mineral wealth, agricultural land, and energy supply for low-margin assembly work. 𝗙𝗮𝗿 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆, 𝗣𝗮𝘅 𝗦𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻’𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘀 𝗮𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗵𝗼𝘀𝘁—𝘀𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗻𝘁𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝘀𝘁.

Undeniably, the state continues to surrender the nation’s vital reserves—enriching foreign monopolies and local elites while the Filipino majority pays the toll in displaced communities and depleted lands.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗣𝗮𝘅 𝗦𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮 𝗳𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀—𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.The establishment of the 4,000-acre Economic Security Zone in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac directly threatens agrarian communities and indigenous populations with displacement, transforming fertile agricultural grounds into an industrial processing hub.

Agricultural advocacy groups like Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) emphasize that giving away vast tracts of land to foreign-backed consortia under the Luzon Economic Corridor is a form of state-sanctioned land grabbing. Instead of investing in genuine agrarian reform and local food sovereignty to feed millions of Filipinos, the state treats rural land as disposable real estate to be handed off to Western technology firms.

When indigenous communities and tenant farmers are pushed off their ancestral lands to make way for foreign-owned data centers and processing plants, it exposes the brutal reality: 𝘁𝗵𝗲 "𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲" 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗣𝗮𝘅 𝗦𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆’𝘀 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗯𝗼𝗻𝗲.

Beyond land displacement, Pax Silica introduces catastrophic environmental risks that will leave lasting scars on local ecosystems. Critical mineral processing—such as extracting and refining nickel, copper, and cobalt needed for advanced circuitry—is notorious for toxic runoff, soil contamination, and heavy metal leaching.

Environmental groups and scientists from the University of the Philippines point out that hosting hyperscale data centers and semiconductor assembly facilities will drain massive amounts of local water and power grids. Data center cooling systems alone consume millions of gallons of water daily, threatening to trigger severe water conflicts in Luzon where local communities already face seasonal water shortages.

The historical precedent is damning: just as former US military bases in Clark and Subic left behind a legacy of uncleaned toxic waste and groundwater contamination, 𝗣𝗮𝘅 𝗦𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝘂𝘇𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝘇𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗴𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀.

While the government boasts that Pax Silica will generate thousands of jobs, a closer look at the electronics sector reveals a pattern of labor exploitation and industrial stagnation. Labor alliances, such as the Metal Workers Alliance of the Philippines (MWAP), point out that the Philippines remains trapped at the absolute bottom of the semiconductor value chain.

The high-value, intellectual-property-heavy stages—such as integrated circuit design, frontier AI model development, and high-margin fabrication—remain strictly locked in Western nations like the US. What the Philippines receives are low-margin, high-hazard jobs in assembly, testing, packaging, and raw mineral extraction.

Filipino workers are subjected to grueling quota systems, exposure to toxic chemicals, and low wages, all while the state suppresses genuine unionization to maintain a "competitive, flexible" labor force. Far from creating a local "Silicon Valley," Pax Silica locks Filipino workers into a cycle of manual, low-wage assembly without transferring high-tech capabilities to the nation.

Ultimately, Pax Silica strips away any romanticized notion of a mutually beneficial "special relationship" between the US and the Philippines, revealing a dangerous military-economic arrangement. Under the banner of "friend-shoring" and the Luzon Economic Corridor, the United States is not offering benevolence; it is securing its own geopolitical dominance against China by turning the Philippines into a forward supply base and mineral buffer zone.

This dynamic encroaches on Philippine national sovereignty, entangling the country deeper into inter-imperialist rivalries and painting a target on critical infrastructure in Tarlac and Clark in the event of regional conflict. By surrendering policy autonomy, land, and critical mineral reserves under terms that prioritize foreign national security over local development, the Philippine government confirms that "friend-shoring" is merely modern neocolonialism—a strategy where foreign powers call the shots, while the host nation bears all the risk.

A country that surrenders its soil, water, and minerals to sustain foreign power is not a partner in progress—it is an exploited host. Pax Silica offers the Philippines the illusion of technological advancement, but the reality is a familiar biological truth: the leech thrives while the body weakens.
Every acre of farmland surrendered in Tarlac and every gallon of water diverted for foreign data centers is a toll paid to maintain an unequal imperialist order. The choice is clear: the country can continue to let foreign monopolies and complicit local elites drain the nation’s vitality, or pull back the diplomatic veneer, reject this parasitic dynamic, and demand a future where Philippine resources serve no one’s interests but its own citizens.

When the host is finally bled dry and its resources exhausted, the parasite does not mourn; it simply moves on to feast elsewhere.

title: Mga progresibong grupo, nagprotesta sa Tarlac sa ika-54 anibersaryo ng Martial Law; proyektong Pax Silica, tinutulan
author: Vincent Jayne B. Pallasigui
excerpt: Bilang pag-alala sa masalimuot na nakaraan at paghiyaw sa pagbabago, nagtipon sa F. Tañedo Street,
body:
Bilang pag-alala sa masalimuot na nakaraan at paghiyaw sa pagbabago, nagtipon sa F. Tañedo Street, Tarlac City ang mga progresibong grupo, akitibista, at residente at katutubo mula Capas, Tarlac para sa isang kilos-protesta kaugnay ng ika-54 anibersaryo ng deklarasyon ng Martial Law sa bansa at upang ipagtanggol ang kanilang lupang ninuno kahapon, September 21.

Kasama ang Kabataang Tarlakenyo para sa Bayan (KTB), Kabataan ng Gitnang Luzon (KGL), at AMBALA, sinimulan ang protesta sa mga pahayag na nagpaalala sa mga inhustiya na dinanas ng mga Pilipino noong panahon ng Batas Militar sa ilalim ng rehimeng Marcos Sr..
Kabilang din sa mga usaping tinalakay ang planong pagtatayo ng data hub na Pax Silica ng Estados Unidos sa New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac na mariing tinutulan, lalo na ng mga residente at katutubong maapektuhan nito.

“Nandito po kami ngayon lumalaban dahil hindi po kami pumapayag. Malaking kawalan po sa aming kalikasan ang kanilang proyekto,” pahayag ni Tatay Nelson, isang katutubo mula Capas na dumalo sa protesta. 

Giit pa niya, paano na lang ang mga magsasaka sa mga lugar na maaapektuhan kung itatayo ang Pax Silica. 

“Hindi naman pag-unlad kundi maraming mahihirapan. Dahil sa aming lupa ay kabundukan at sa kalikasan, maraming maapektuhan. Kami po ay hindi pumapayag at lumalaban dahil hindi lang po kami at mga magsasaka [ang madadamay],” ani Tatay Nelson.

“Kami po ay sama-samang kumikilos upang maipahayag sa gobyerno na huwag pong gawin sa amin iyon dahil ginagalang po namin sila. dapat matuto silang gumalang sa aming mga katutubo,” dagdag pa niya.

Kasunod nito, nagmartsa ang raliyista patungo sa tapat ng Downtown Market, kung saan nagbigay ng pahayag ang mga biktima ng Martial Law, mga kasamahang katutubo, at ang mga estudyante-aktibista.

Sa pagpapatuloy ng protesta, naramdaman ang presensya ng kapulisan at ilang miyembro ng Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) na nakabantay sa kahabaan ng daan. 

Sa kabila nito, hindi natinag ang mga raliyista at pansin ang paglakas ng kanilang sound system habang isinisigaw ang mga panawagan ng taumbayan. 

“Hindi na bago ang barikada sa mga lansangan upang harangan ang mga raliyista,” saad ni John Mc Miel Guerero, isa sa mga estudyante-aktibista mula Tarlac Satate University (TSU), sa isang panayam.

Panawagan niya sa mga iskolar ng bayan na pagsilbihan ang taumbayan. “I-exercise natin ang ating academic freedom. Pag-aralan ang lipunan. Through rallies, sa pakikilahok sa mga ganitong programa ay masusuklian natin ‘yung hirap na ginagawa ng mga nagbabayad ng buwis.”

“Sa mga kabataan na gustong sumali sa mga ganitong programa ay huwag kayong matakot na makibaka dahil ito ay karapatan natin bilang Pilipino,” dagdag pa niya.

Bukod sa Tarlac, nagkasa rin ng kaparehong kilos ang iba’t ibang progresibong grupo at kabataan sa iba’t ibang parte ng bansa bilang pag-alala sa Martial Law at upang tutulan ang lumalalang pasismo.

title: Katutubo, progresibong grupo nagkaisa; naglunsad ng alyansa kontra Pax Silica
author: Janeth G. Gamboa
excerpt: Katutubo, progresibong grupo nagkaisa; naglunsad ng alyansa kontra Pax Silica Kasabay ng paggunita ng Araw ng mga Bayani, mahigit 200 mula sa higit 70 organisasyon sa Mary Hill School of Theology sa Quezon City ang dumalo…
body:
Kasabay ng paggunita ng Araw ng mga Bayani, mahigit 200 mula sa higit 70 organisasyon sa Mary Hill School of Theology sa Quezon City ang dumalo sa pormal na paglunsad sa Network Opposed to Pax Silica (NO to Pax Silica), isang alyansang kumokontra sa US-led Pax Silica initiative at ang pagtatag ng Economic Security Zone (ESZ) sa New Clark City, Tarlac, Agosto 31.

Nagsama-sama sa paglunsad ang mga katutubong Ayta at mga magsasaka mula sa Tarlac, mga environmental, peace, at human rights advocates, kabataan at estudyante, faith-based groups, at iba pang sektor upang talakayin ang mga epekto ng Pax Silica.

𝗞𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗯𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝘆𝘁𝗮, 𝘁𝘂𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗴

Isa sa pangunahing tampok ng programa ang panel discussion hinggil sa iba’t ibang usapin na nakapalibot sa 1,600-ektaryang development project, kabilang ang land grabbing, displacement, environmental degradation, resource extraction, developmental priorities, national sovereignty, at peace.

Tinalakay ni Apung Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, Ayta Chieftain ng Sitio Sapang Kawayan sa Capas, Tarlac, ang pangambang mawala ang kanilang lupa at kabuhayan dahil sa mga plano sa kanilang ancestral domain.
Ayon kay Capiz-Muñoz, binigyan umano ng Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) ang kanilang komunidad ng hanggang Disyembre upang lisanin ang kanilang lupang ninuno.

Aniya, hindi umano ipinaliwanag sa kanila kung anong partikular na proyekto ang itatayo sa kanilang lupa at nalaman na lamang nila sa social media na ito pala ay ang Pax Silica na itatayo sa New Clark City.

"Alam niyo naman po kung sino at sa amin na ang lupa ay buhay po namin... Paano po ang aming kabuhayan kung mawawala ang aming lupa at gagawing proyekto ng Pax Silica? Kaya po kami andito ngayon, nananawagan po sa inyo. Paulit-ulit na naman po ang mga pangyayari," ani Capit-Muñoz.

Dagdag pa ni Capiz-Muñoz, nagsimula nang makaranas ng harassment mula sa militar ang ilang miyembro ng kanilang katutubo dahil sa pagtutol sa proyekto.

Ibinahagi rin niya ang naging karanasan ng kanilang komunidad noong 2019 bago magsimula ang COVID-19 pandemic, nang sinabihan umano silang lumisan sa kanilang ancestral lands sa loob ng pitong araw kasabay ng pagsisimula ng clearing operations sa kanilang kabundukan.

Sa halip na sumunod, nagtayo ang mga katutubo ng mga harang upang pigilan ang pagpapatuloy ng clearing operation. Gayunman, nagpatuloy ang pagkasira ng bahagi ng kanilang kabundukan.

Ayon sa kaniya, ang ilang sagradong bundok at kuweba na mahalaga sa kanilang komunidad ay naapektuhan ng mga development project at ginawang bahagi ng mga bagong pasilidad gaya ng golf course, resorts, at hotels.

Binigyang-diin ng lider-Ayta na ang lupang kanilang ipinaglalaban ay hindi lamang tirahan kundi pangunahing pinagkukunan ng pagkain, kabuhayan, at iba pang pangangailangan.

“Mawawala kami lahat, paano na lang ang aming salinlahi?” ani niya.

𝗔𝗜 𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲

Tinalakay naman ni Dr. Giovanni Tapang, Chair Emeritus ng Advocates for Sciences and Technology for the People (AGHAM) at dating Dean ng UP Diliman College of Science, ang papel ng mga yamang mineral sa Pax Silica at ang kaugnayan nito sa pandaigdigang kompetisyon sa teknolohiya.

Ayon kay Tapang, mahalagang maunawaan kung kaninong pangunahing interes ang silbi ng Pax Silica, lalo na sa gitna ng patuloy na tunggalian ng Estados Unidos at China sa artificial intelligence (AI) at sa semiconductor technology. Kasama na rito na nais maunahan ng US ang China sa produksiyon ng AI chips.

“Itong Pax Silica na ito malinaw na sa US na mismo sinabi para sa interes ng US,” ani Tapang.
Dagdag pa ni Tapang, hindi lamang paggawa ng computer chips ang nakapaloob sa usapin kundi maging ang pagkuha at pagproseso ng mga mineral at pagtatayo ng mga data center. 

Ibinahagi rin niya ang mga pangamba hinggil sa posibleng epekto ng proyekto sa suplay ng tubig at kuryente. Nabanggit din niya ang kakailanganing pagtayo ng water collection facility dahil sa malaking pangangailangan ng AI hub sa tubig na inaasahang aabot sa 60-90 milyong litro kada araw.

Itinaas din sa diskusyon ang pangangalap at konsentrasyon ng mga rare earth minerals, kabilang ang radioactive minerals gaya ng thorium, gayundin ang posibleng hamon sa waste management.

𝗨𝗦-𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗮 𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗿𝘆

Samantala, iginiit ni Teddy Casiño, chairperson ng Bagong Alyansang Makabayan, na hindi dapat tignan ang Pax Silica bilang isang simpleng programang pang-ekonomiya, ngunit isang malawak na heopolitikal na konteksto.

Ayon kay Casiño, ipiniprisinta ang proyekto bilang oportunidad para makapasok ang Pilipinas sa global AI supply chain, makahikayat ng investments, makalikha ng mga trabaho, at makasabay sa pag-unlad ng teknolohiya.

“Pero dapat nating maunawaan na ang Pax Silica ay higit pa sa usapin sa ekonomiya. Ito ay bunga ng tumitinding tungalian sa pagitan ng US at China para kontrolin ang pinakamodernong teknolohiya at sa muli para kontrolin ang pandaigdigang ekonomiya,” ani Casiño.

Binigyang-pansin din niya ang koneksyon ng kompetisyon sa AI sa kompetisyong pangmilitar kung saan tinawag niyang isang “weaponization” ng Philippine industrial development ang planong proyekto.

Ayon kay Casiño, bahagi ng estratehiya ng Estados Unidos ang pagpapalakas ng tinatawag na “First Island Chain” laban sa China kung saan maaring magsilbi ang Pilipinas hindi lamang bilang bahagi ng global technology supply chain kundi lokasyon para sa mga US military bases.

Idiniin din niya ang panganib na maaaring harapin ng bansa sakaling lumala ang tensyon sa pagitan ng Estados Unidos at China, partikular na sa usapin ng Taiwan Strait.

Para kay Casiño, kailangang mapanatili ng Pilipinas ang kakayahang magpasya para sa sariling industriyalisasyon, paggamit ng likas na yaman, at kinabukasan ng bansa at hindi maging daluyan ng kontrol ng ibang bansa.

“Ang industriyalisasyon ng Pilipinas ay dapat para sa Pilipinas, ang soberanya ng Pilipinas ay dapat manatili sa mga Pilipino, at ang kinabukasan ng Pilipinas ay dapat tayong mga Pilipino ang magpapasya.”

𝗪𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗸𝗶, 𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗮𝗻

Nagbigay din ng recorded video statement si Miss Universe Philippines 2026 Bea Millan-Windorski, kung saan ipinahayag niya ang pagtutol sa panukalang Pax Silica at ang pag-alala sa posibleng epekto nito sa mga magsasaka, katutubo, at kalikasan sa Tarlac.

Sa kaniyang pahayag, sinabi ni Windorski na bagamat may mga assurance umano mula sa BCDA na hindi maapektuhan ang mga bukiran, may mga ulat na 92 magsasaka sa Barangay O’Donnell, Capas, Tarlac ang hinihikayat nang lisanin ang lupang kanilang sinasaka. Binanggit din niya ang ulat na nasa 500 pamilya sa Barangay Sta. Lucia, Capas, Tarlac ang maaaring maapektuhan ng proyekto.

Ayon kay Windorski, hindi lamang pagkawala ng kabuhayan ang dapat pagtuunan ng pansin kundi maging ang posibleng epekto sa mga indigenous communities na matagal nang nangangalaga sa lupain.

“This National Heroes Day, may we remember that our true heroes are reflected in the faces of the indigenous, the minor, subsistence farmers and the marginalized,” pahayag ni Windorski.

(Ngayong Araw ng mga Bayani, alahanin natin na ang ating tunay na mga bayani ay makikita sa mga mukha ng mga katutubo, ang minorya, magsasakang nagsusumikap, at sa mga nasa laylayan.)

Ayon sa NO to Pax Silica, kabilang sa kanilang mga unang hakbang ang pagbisita sa mga katutubo at farming communities na sinasabing maapektuhan ng ESZ sa Capas, Tarlac. Plano rin ng alyansa na magsagawa ng mga public forum upang palawakin pa ang diskusyon hinggil sa Pax Silica at sa mga posibleng epekto nito.

Samantala, inaasahang lalagda ang Pilipinas at Estados Unidos sa isang pormal na framework agreement sa Pax Silica sa Nobyembre, na posibleng isabay sa pagdaraos ng ASEAN Summit sa Maynila.
